summary: Describes the Media Gateway Control Protocol, an interface and protocol used between parts of a decomposed multimedia gateway. A Call Agent holds the call control logic while media gateways handle conversion such as TDM voice to voice over IP, and the Call Agent controls the gateway's endpoints. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MGCP lets a Call Agent control a media gateway, which converts telephone signals into media carried over packet networks. The Call Agent tells the gateway's endpoints when to create connections and which events to report. RFC 3435 is Informational and points to RFC 3015 as the standards-based approach for the same needs.

subtitle: How a Call Agent controls media gateways and their telephone endpoints.

tldr.problem: A multimedia gateway needs to connect telephone-side endpoints to packet-network media, while call control can be handled separately from media conversion.
tldr.mechanism: MGCP lets a Call Agent send commands to a media gateway's endpoints to create, change, and delete connections, request event reports, and inspect endpoint state.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3435 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 2705, and is updated by RFC 3661. Its IESG note points to RFC 3015 as the standards-based way to meet the needs MGCP was designed to address.

sections.title: Separating Call Control from Media
sections.content:
RFC 3435 defines the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) and an abstract interface for controlling media gateways. A Call Agent holds the call-control logic. A media gateway handles media functions, such as converting voice carried on telephone circuits into Voice over IP packets.

The gateway contains endpoints that can detect events, play signals, and carry connections. MGCP is a master/slave protocol: gateways execute commands from Call Agents. The RFC does not define how multiple Call Agents synchronize, so they must coordinate to send consistent commands.

The RFC is Informational, not an Internet Standard. Its IESG note says implementers should be aware of RFC 3015, which the IETF and ITU-T consider the standards-based way to meet the needs MGCP was designed to address.
sections.plainLanguage: MGCP separates call decisions from the work of converting and carrying media. A Call Agent makes the decisions, and the gateway follows its commands. The RFC does not define how multiple Call Agents coordinate with one another.

sections.title: Endpoints, Connections and Calls
sections.content:
An endpoint is a source or destination for data. It can represent a physical interface, such as an analog telephone line or digital channel, or a virtual resource, such as an audio source in an announcement server. A connection links endpoints or joins an endpoint to a multipoint session. Connections can carry media over RTP and UDP on IP, over AAL2 on ATM, or over a gateway's internal path.

One or more connections can be grouped into a call. The Call Agent creates a hexadecimal call identifier, up to 32 characters long; MGCP gives it little meaning beyond compatibility and accounting or management. The gateway creates a hexadecimal connection identifier, also up to 32 characters long. It must wait at least 3 minutes before reusing that identifier on the same endpoint.

Endpoint names combine a local name and the gateway's domain name, in the form local-endpoint-name@domain-name. The local name can use slash-separated levels. An asterisk selects all matching values, while a dollar sign selects any one matching value, normally an endpoint in service.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint is a place where media enters or leaves a gateway. A connection links endpoints, and a call can group one or more connections. Each endpoint name identifies both the endpoint and the gateway that manages it.

sections.title: Commands, Events and Signals
sections.content:
MGCP defines nine commands. Call Agents use EndpointConfiguration to set line-side coding; NotificationRequest to ask for event detection and signals; CreateConnection, ModifyConnection, and DeleteConnection to manage connections; and AuditEndpoint and AuditConnection to inspect state. Gateways use Notify to report detected events and RestartInProgress to report service changes.

An event is something an endpoint detects, such as a hook transition or a dialed digit. A signal is something it produces, such as ringing or dial tone. A NotificationRequest can say which events to watch for, what to do with each event, and which signals to apply. The gateway reports requested events in a Notify command, which repeats the request identifier so the Call Agent can match the report to its request.

Packages group events, signals, and other extensions for endpoint types. A digit map lets the Call Agent give the gateway patterns for collecting digits; the gateway reports the collected string when it matches a pattern or cannot match one.
sections.plainLanguage: The Call Agent can ask an endpoint to watch for an event, such as a phone going off-hook, or to produce a signal, such as ringing. The gateway reports requested events with a Notify command. Packages define which events and signals an endpoint supports.

sections.title: Creating and Changing Connections
sections.content:
For two endpoints on gateways managed by the same Call Agent, MGCP uses a three-step setup. The Call Agent asks the first gateway to create a connection and receives its session description, which includes information such as an IP address, UDP port, and codec parameters. It passes that description to the second gateway in another CreateConnection command, receives the second description, then sends that description to the first gateway in a ModifyConnection command. Media can then flow in both directions.

When both endpoints are on one gateway, CreateConnection can name the second endpoint instead of carrying a remote session description. The gateway creates two separately managed connections. A connection's mode controls how media is sent, received, mixed, or looped back; the RFC defines modes including send-only, receive-only, send/receive, conference, inactive, and continuity-test modes.

ModifyConnection can change a connection's mode, remote description, or local media options. DeleteConnection removes it and can return media statistics. When a CreateConnection or ModifyConnection includes a NotificationRequest, both operations must succeed or both must be refused.
sections.plainLanguage: To connect endpoints on two gateways, the Call Agent collects a session description from each gateway and gives each side the information it needs about the other. It then tells the first gateway to use the second description. The gateways can exchange media after that setup is complete.

sections.title: Text Messages and Transaction Replies
sections.content:
MGCP commands and responses are text lines separated by carriage return and line feed, or by a line feed. A command begins with a four-letter verb, a transaction identifier, an endpoint name, and the protocol version. Parameter lines follow; an optional session description comes after an empty line. The command grammar is case-insensitive except for the session description.

Each command receives a response with a return code. Codes from 000 to 099 acknowledge a response, 100 to 199 are provisional, 200 to 299 mean success, 400 to 499 indicate transient errors, and 500 to 599 indicate permanent errors. Codes from 800 to 899 are package-specific.

MGCP uses UDP, which can lose messages. To prevent a repeated command from running twice, each entity remembers recent responses and resends the stored response when it sees a duplicate transaction identifier. Retransmission timers use exponential backoff. The RFC suggests a 30-second history timer and a 4-second maximum retransmission timer, and requires implementations to accept MGCP datagrams of at least 4000 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command has a transaction number, and its reply repeats that number. If a command is repeated because its reply may have been lost, the gateway resends its saved reply instead of doing the work again. Reply codes show whether the command is still running, succeeded, or failed.

sections.title: Failover, Restarts and Event Timing
sections.content:
Each endpoint has one current notified entity, the Call Agent to which it sends commands. A Call Agent can change this value with a NotifiedEntity parameter. Domain names can resolve to multiple network addresses; if one address cannot be reached, entities must try another. The RFC assumes separate Call Agents coordinate their actions and does not define conflict resolution when control is handed between them.

When a gateway cannot contact its Call Agent after retries, it treats the endpoint as disconnected and sends RestartInProgress using the disconnected method. Restart methods also include graceful, forced, restart, and cancel-graceful. A gateway uses a randomized delay when restarting so many gateways do not contact the Call Agent at once.

While a Notify is awaiting a response, the gateway stores detected events in a first-in, first-out quarantine buffer. A later NotificationRequest determines whether it processes or discards those events. The RFC also gives rules for command ordering, cancelled transactions, and limiting traffic when a Call Agent or gateway is overloaded.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint sends reports to one current Call Agent. If that Call Agent cannot be reached, the gateway retries and reports that the endpoint is disconnected. During a restart, a randomized delay helps prevent many gateways from contacting the Call Agent at the same time.

sections.title: Protecting Commands and Media
sections.content:
Any entity can send a command to an MGCP endpoint, so an unauthorized sender could set up calls or interfere with authorized calls. The RFC expects MGCP messages to use the IP security architecture and says gateways and Call Agents should accept only messages authenticated by IP security. It names the IP Authentication Header and IP Encapsulating Security Payload as options.

Encryption can also help prevent eavesdropping on connections. The Call Agent can provide session keys for encrypting audio. Without media protection, an attacker who sends packets to a connection's IP address and UDP port could inject audio that is played on the telephone side. The RFC describes encryption and packet authentication with a setup key as stronger protection against source spoofing than checking source addresses alone.

The RFC notes that these measures do not necessarily prevent denial-of-service attacks by a misbehaving gateway or Call Agent, but can identify the entity so its authorization can be withdrawn.
sections.plainLanguage: MGCP commands need authentication because an unauthorized sender could create or disrupt calls. The RFC calls for IP security to authenticate messages. Encrypting and authenticating media can help prevent eavesdropping and injected audio.

sections.title: Packages, Compatibility and Status
sections.content:
Packages are MGCP's preferred extension method. A package can define events, signals, actions, connection modes, parameters, restart methods, and return codes. Package names are registered with IANA unless they use the reserved experimental prefixes x- or x+. A new version of a package must remain backward-compatible; an incompatible extension needs a new package name.

RFC 3435 updates the earlier MGCP specification, RFC 2705, with implementation clarifications and changes to naming, digit maps, event handling, transactions, failover, security, and package extensions. The unit metadata records that RFC 3435 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 2705, and is updated by RFC 3661. The IESG note points implementers to RFC 3015 as the standards-based way to meet the needs MGCP was designed to address.
sections.plainLanguage: Packages let MGCP add features for different endpoint types while keeping each extension named and defined. A new package version must keep earlier features working. RFC 3435 is Informational, replaces RFC 2705, and the RFC's IESG note points to RFC 3015 for the standards-based approach.
